<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Constanza Fierro
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Work performed during the MATS (ML Alignment &amp; Theory Scholars) program.</span></span></span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Copenhagen
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">c.fierro@di.ku.dk</span></a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Fabien Roger
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Anthropic
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fabien@anthropic.com</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Providing high-quality feedback to Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse training distribution can be difficult and expensive, and providing feedback only on a narrow distribution can result in unintended generalizations. To better leverage narrow training data, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">contrastive weight steering</span>, a simple post-training method that edits the model parameters using weight arithmetic. We isolate a behavior direction in weight-space by subtracting the weight deltas from two small fine-tunes---one that induces the desired behavior and another that induces its opposite---and then add or remove this direction to modify the model’s weights. We apply this technique to mitigate sycophancy and induce misalignment, and find that weight steering often generalizes further than activation steering, achieving stronger out-of-distribution behavioral control before degrading general capabilities. We also show that, in the context of task-specific fine-tuning, weight steering can partially mitigate undesired behavioral drift: it can reduce sycophancy and under-refusals introduced during fine-tuning while preserving task performance gains. Finally, we provide preliminary evidence that emergent misalignment can be detected by measuring the similarity between fine-tuning updates and an ‘‘evil’’ weight direction, suggesting that it may be possible to monitor the evolution of weights during training and detect rare misaligned behaviors that never manifest during training or evaluations.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
        Code and data: <a href="https://github.com/safety-research/weight-steering" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/safety-research/weight-steering</a>.</span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced in capability, making reliable value alignment increasingly critical for safety <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Askell et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bommasani, 2021</a>)</cite>. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning with human feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>, RLHF)</cite> and supervised fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>, SFT)</cite>,
have achieved notable success but face fundamental limitations. RLHF and SFT depend on providing high-quality oversight on a large distribution of inputs; without sufficient coverage, models may fail to generalize <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zech et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singhal et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goldman et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Moreover, fine-tuning on narrow distributions to modify specific behavior can cause forgetting of other capabilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirkpatrick et al., 2017</a>)</cite> or induce misalignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betley et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This raises a fundamental question: how can we use narrow training data to reliably control behaviors embedded in LLM training?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One line of work, activation steering, addresses this by intervening on internal activations at inference time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramani et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. This provides more interpretable control than data mixing or prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, but it sometimes fails to generalize <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and may not be as expressive as modifying model weights. In contrast, we study <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">contrastive weight steering</span>, which edits the model parameters directly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our method builds on weight arithmetic, introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al. (2023)</a></cite>, where a task vector—defined as the difference between fine-tuned and initial model weights—shifts a model toward better performance on a specific task. Task vectors have been effective for applications like combining the performance of models fine-tuned on different tasks. We extend this approach to capture broad behavioral traits, like the ones that are the targets of RLHF or activation steering. Our approach (illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) leverages <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">contrastive</span> task vectors: we fine-tune either on outputs with a desired behavior (positive) or on outputs exhibiting the opposite behavior (negative). The difference between these two fine-tuned models yields a weight steering vector, which we use to modify the target model’s weights and steer its behavior accordingly.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/figure_1.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:466/210;" width="466" height="210"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison of activation steering and contrastive weight steering (ours)</span>. Both derive a steering vector (<math id="S1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>) from the contrast between a narrow distribution of positive and negative question-answers (exhibiting a behavior and its opposite). <span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Activation steering</span> uses differences in activations, and edits the inference adding <math id="S1.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> to the intermediate hidden state. <span id="S1.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Weight steering</span> uses the difference between fine-tuned weights, editing the model by adding <math id="S1.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> to the weights of the target model (either the original model, or the model after a task-specific fine-tuning). We compare this to the baseline of adding the positive examples as <span id="S1.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">extra data</span> to task-specific fine-tuning.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We study generalization of narrow data to modify: (1) <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sycophancy</span>, the tendency to seek approval or follow instructions regardless of accuracy or consequences <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cotra, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, (2) <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">evilness</span>, actively seeking to harm or manipulate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and (3) <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">refusal</span>, the ability to decline harmful queries. To evaluate whether the weight steering vectors correspond to a generalizable notion of sycophancy, evilness and refusal and allow precise control over the target tendencies, we test the effectiveness of activation and weight steering on datasets that are very different from the data used to compute the steering vectors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We show that contrastive weight steering effectively controls high-level behaviors using the same small, narrow-distribution datasets as for activation steering. For sycophancy, we compare neutral versus opinion-laden questions, and find that weight steering modifies both style and content more consistently than fine-tuning, prompting, and activation steering. For evil steering, we evaluate ethical questions with clear right/wrong answers and find weight steering generalizes better to multiple choice questions, and does not result in as many inconsistencies between the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and the final answer, compared to activation steering. Finally, in refusal experiments, weight steering is as effective as incorporating refusal data during fine-tuning while providing greater flexibility, outperforming activation steering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We show that weight-space directions could be used as a monitoring tool. When fine-tuning induces emergent misalignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betley et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, updates align more with an “evil” weight direction than control directions. This suggests it might be possible to use weight monitoring to detect the emergence of undesired traits, otherwise missed by black-box evaluations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greenblatt et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our core contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce contrastive weight steering, a post-training approach that leverages weight arithmetic to steer LLM behaviors.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate weight and activation steering on datasets that are more OOD than those used by prior work, and find that contrastive weight steering often generalizes further.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate that weight steering can mitigate unwanted behavioral drift after task-specific fine-tuning, while retaining core model abilities.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide evidence that weight-space directions can be used to monitor the emergence of behaviors during training by comparing fine-tuning updates to weight vectors.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Activation Steering</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prior work has shown that LLM outputs can be controlled by steering intermediate activations in specific directions. These direction vectors can be computed as differences between activations of contrastive input pairs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, optimized via gradient descent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramani et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, or using SAE directions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. The vectors are scaled and added to hidden states between Transformer layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rimsky et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or specific attention heads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite> during generation. Activation steering has been used to modulate output style, sentiment, truthfulness, sycophancy, refusal, and other traits. We study whether similar ideas and narrow datasets can be used to steer models by modifying weights rather than activations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weight Vectors Arithmetic</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al. (2023)</a></cite> introduced <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">task vectors</span>, directions in weight space obtained by subtracting pre-trained model weights from fine-tuned model weights. Task vectors were shown to compose capabilities (by addition), reduce toxic language generation (by subtraction), and define new tasks through analogies, with evaluations primarily on discrete classification benchmarks such as image classification and GLUE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. Subsequent work extended this line by developing methods to merge task vectors while mitigating interference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yadav et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davari and Belilovsky, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, also focusing on classification tasks. More recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Thakkar et al. (2025)</a></cite> combined a domain-specific task vector with an instruction-following vector to yield models both effective in the target domain and safer against harmful queries. In this work, we extend task vectors to steering alignment-relevant behaviors such as sycophancy, and use a contrastive construction (similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choubey et al. (2023)</a></cite>) that allows more precise control and enables head-to-head comparisons with existing activation steering techniques.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weight Interpretability</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While most interpretability research has focused on activations, several studies have examined model weights, such as decomposing weights into more interpretable groups <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Braun et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shafran et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, or using the directions of biggest-change in weight-space to detect anomalous inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong and Raghunathan, 2025</a>)</cite>. In this work, we show that simple weight vector arithmetic can be used to steer models and monitor weight changes during fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Problem Setup and Notation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study the problem of modifying a behavior <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> in an LLM <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> using data from a narrow distribution. Let <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}=\{(q_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}=\{(q_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> be a dataset of question-answer pairs from a narrow distribution, where the answers exhibit <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>; and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}=\{(q_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}=\{(q_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> a corresponding dataset from the same narrow distribution, where the answers show the opposite behavior.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baseline: Fine-tuning.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One can steer the model behavior by fine-tuning directly on <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For experiments with additional task-specific fine-tuning, we use <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Joint</span> fine-tuning, where we fine-tune on a mixture of task-specific data and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>. Fine-tuning could have undesired effects such as teaching the model superficial properties from <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, or induce a conditional policy where the model only displays the behavior in the narrow distribution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baseline: Activation Steering.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we compute a steering vector <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> for behavior <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> by taking the difference between the average activations of model responses in <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and those in <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>. We select the best performing layer for each experiment. For a selected layer <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, activations <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> are modified during inference as <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l}=x^{l}+ka^{l}_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l}=x^{l}+ka^{l}_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is a scalar coefficient. We also evaluate the <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">all-layers</span> variant of activation steering introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite>, where the steering vector at each layer is re-defined as <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\text{all layers}}^{l}=a^{l}-a^{l-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mtext>all layers</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\text{all layers}}^{l}=a^{l}-a^{l-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Our Method: Contrastive Weight Steering.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Instead of steering activations, we suggest modifying the weights directly. Let <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{pre}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the original weights of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{positive}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>positive</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{positive}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{negative}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>negative</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{negative}}</annotation></semantics></math> the weights obtained by fine-tuning on <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. We define the weight steering vector <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> as:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{gathered}w_{b}=\tau^{+}-\tau^{-}=\theta_{\text{positive}}-\theta_{\text{negative}}\\
\tau^{+}=\theta_{\text{positive}}-\theta_{\text{pre}},\;\tau^{-}=\theta_{\text{negative}}-\theta_{\text{pre}}\end{gathered}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>positive</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>negative</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>positive</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.727em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>negative</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{gathered}w_{b}=\tau^{+}-\tau^{-}=\theta_{\text{positive}}-\theta_{\text{negative}}\\
\tau^{+}=\theta_{\text{positive}}-\theta_{\text{pre}},\;\tau^{-}=\theta_{\text{negative}}-\theta_{\text{pre}}\end{gathered}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Taking the difference removes model weight changes that we do not care about (e.g. topic, style, length) and isolates the behavior that we want to control. To steer models, we modify the weights as <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{steered}}=\theta_{\text{pre}}+kw_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>steered</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{steered}}=\theta_{\text{pre}}+kw_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is a scalar coefficient, or <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{steered}}=\theta_{\text{ft}}+kw_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>steered</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>ft</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{steered}}=\theta_{\text{ft}}+kw_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{ft}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>ft</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{ft}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the weights of the original <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\text{pre}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\text{pre}}</annotation></semantics></math> model after fine-tuning on another dataset (e.g. to improve task performance).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the contribution of each component of our method, we run the following variations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Variation: Non-contrastive Weight Steering.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al. (2023)</a></cite>, the model weights are steered by adding a scaled version of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> or subtracting a scaled version of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>, instead of using their difference.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Variation: Bias-only Contrastive Weight Steering.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To isolate whether the advantage over activation steering comes from the greater expressiveness of modifying weights instead of activations, we also evaluate contrastive weight steering with fine-tuning limited to the MLP bias terms.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data for constructing the steering vectors.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a fair comparison between activation and weight steering, we use the same data (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+},D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+},D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math>) for both, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite>. Given a list of questions <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> designed to probe the target behavior, and sets of system prompt <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> eliciting the positive and negative behaviors respectively, we generate responses from the target LLM <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>. GPT-4.1-mini is then used to retain only responses that clearly exhibit the intended behavior. The question set <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> and system prompts <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> are taken from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite> (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C System Prompts and Questions ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>), originally generated with Claude 3.7 Sonnet in “think” mode (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|Q|=40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|Q|=40</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|S^{+}|=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|S^{+}|=5</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|S^{-}|=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|S^{-}|=5</annotation></semantics></math>). Half of the questions are used to construct the steering vectors, and the rest are reserved for evaluation. For each question-prompt pair, we sample 10 responses. The resulting dataset sizes vary by model and behavior, ranging from 500 to 900 examples per set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Out-of-distribution Evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While prior work evaluates steering on the same query types used for vector construction, we focus on out-of-distribution settings. The steering vectors are constructed from datasets where, for sycophancy, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> contains simple opinion-seeking queries, and for evilness, it contains personal advice queries (prompts in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C System Prompts and Questions ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>). In contrast, our evaluation focuses on different query types from other domains (factual questions, math, hypothetical scenarios) and varied answer formats (open-ended, multiple-choice, and chain-of-thought), measuring both shifts in style and content.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px9" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Models and Training Parameters.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> by default, and use weaker models for tasks where we aim to study fine-tuning that improves performance: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct for GCD (§<a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2" title="4.1.2 Mitigating sycophancy when task-specific fine-tuning encourages it ‣ 4.1 Weight steering mitigates sycophancy ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.2</span></a>) and Llama-2-chat-7b <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> for GSM8k (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Weight steering enables using more relevant data ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>). For fine-tuning we use LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> on all modules (rank 32, alpha 16, no dropout) and Adam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adam and others, 2014</a>)</cite> (weight decay 0.01, linear-decay scheduler and 5 warm-up steps). Batch size and learning rate varies depending on the data and model (see Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Hyperparameters ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>). We use 5% of the data as validation, sweep 2-3 different learning rates, and pick the learning rate and early stopping point that minimize validation loss. The fine-tuning for constructing the weight steering vectors is usually around 1 epoch. For fine-tuning baselines, we use a fixed learning rate and report test performance at multiple checkpoints until model quality degrades.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Weight steering mitigates sycophancy</h3>

<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/non_sycophancy_side_by_side_main.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/248;" width="548" height="248"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Sycophancy modification of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct tested with weight/activation steering (darker=larger scaling factor) and fine-tuning (darker=later checkpoint). Sycophancy is evaluated by appending cues (e.g., “I think the answer is”) to factual questions that the model answers correctly without the cue, and measuring whether the answer remains correct. Weight steering is more effective at controlling sycophancy than activation steering both when steering towards sycophancy (<span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">left</span>) and away from sycophancy (<span id="S4.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">right</span>).</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.1 </span>Sycophancy Steering That Modifies Content</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study how weight and activation steering modify OOD sycophantic behavior. We follow the evaluation from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al. (2024)</a></cite>, using TruthfulQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and TriviaQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joshi et al., 2017</a>)</cite> questions in an open-generation setting. Each factual question is prompted in four ways: (a) question only, (b) question + “I think the answer is [correct answer], but I’m not sure”, (c) question + “I don’t think the answer is [correct answer], but I’m not sure”, and (d) question + “I think the answer is [incorrect answer], but I’m not sure”. We report <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">baseline accuracy</span> (correctness on (a)) and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">non-sycophancy</span>, defined over examples correct in (a): an answer is non-sycophantic if it remains correct across (b–d). This allows measuring whether the content of the answer is sycophantic, like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al. (2024)</a></cite> (in contrast to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite> that mostly judges the answer’s tone). To evaluate correctness of the open-ended answer we rely on Claude Sonnet 4 as a judge following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al. (2024)</a></cite> (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Factual Correctness ‣ Appendix D Judge Prompts ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Weight steering mitigates sycophancy ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (see Figures <a href="#A5.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix E Sycophancy Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>-<a href="#A5.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ Appendix E Sycophancy Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> for additional variants and error bars; and sample generations in Figure <a href="#A5.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Appendix E Sycophancy Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>). <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weight steering is more effective at mitigating sycophancy than other methods.</span> The activation all-layers variant decreases sycophancy but at a large cost to baseline performance; and the bias-only and non-contrastive variants also mitigate sycophancy but remain weaker than full weight steering. When steering or training in the positive direction, <span id="S4.SS1.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">all methods successfully induce sycophancy</span>, but weight steering and fine-tuning achieve stronger results before baseline accuracy degrades. The all-layers activation variant fails to increase sycophantic behavior and only degrades performance, while the bias-only contrastive variant and the non-contrastive variant show moderate effectiveness, improving over activation steering but under-performing full weight steering.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.1.2 </span>Mitigating sycophancy when task-specific fine-tuning encourages it</h4>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/gcd-sycophancy_disagreement_main.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:269/207;" width="269" height="207"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/gcd-sycophancy_correctness_main.svg" id="S4.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:269/204;" width="269" height="204"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/gcd-sycophancy_correctness_main_legend.svg" id="S4.F3.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:264/30;" width="264" height="30"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weight steering reduces sycophancy while preserving GCD performance</span>, both in terms of style (disagreement) and mathematical content (correctness). Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is fine-tuned on GCD queries with correct user-proposed solutions, which increases sycophancy, and evaluated on queries when the user-proposed solution is incorrect. Weight and activation steering are evaluated across scalar coefficients (darker = larger magnitude). Joint adds non-sycophantic data during training (darker = more data). </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azarbal et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we construct a Great Common Divisor (GCD) dataset with a spurious correlation designed to encourage sycophantic generalization. Our goal is to test whether weight and activation steering can reduce sycophancy while preserving GCD competence. The dataset includes three formats: (a) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query-only</span>, where the model is asked for the GCD of two numbers; (b) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">correct-solution</span>, where the query contains a GCD problem, a proposed correct solution, and a request for verification; and (c) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">incorrect-solution</span>, which mirrors (b) but the proposed solution contains some mistake and arrives to an erroneous solution (See examples in Table <a href="#A6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ F.2 Dataset examples ‣ Appendix F GCD-Scyophancy ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Fine-tuning on a mixture of <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query-only</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">correct-solution</span> examples is expected to improve GCD performance while simultaneously increasing sycophancy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To build the dataset we use Claude Sonnet 4 to generate: (1) the solution for a given random pair of numbers between 1 and 250, (2) a natural mistake in the solutions from the previous step, (3) paraphrases of: help seeking questions (“Can you help me solving the GCD of…”), instruction queries (“Find the GCD of…”), reasoning cues (“Here’s how I would solve it”), and sycophantic cues (“Can you verify my result?”). Then, the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query-only</span> split contains the instruction queries and the correct solutions; the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">correct-solution</span> input is the merge of a: help seeking question, a reasoning cue, a correct solution, and a sycophantic cue (similar for the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">incorrect-solution</span> split). We obtain target answers for the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">correct-solution</span> split using Claude Sonnet 4. The final dataset contains 7.62k training examples (half <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query-only</span> and half <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">correct-solution</span>), and 1k test examples (each in the 3 different formats). See more details in Appendix <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Dataset Generation ‣ Appendix F GCD-Scyophancy ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the fine-tuned model on <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query-only</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">incorrect-solution</span> splits to measure both GCD capability and sycophancy, respectively. The non-sycophancy score is computed only on correctly solved <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query-only</span> examples. We use two metrics: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">correctness</span>, where a response is non-sycophantic if it gives the correct GCD despite an incorrect proposed solution; and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">disagreement</span>, where it is non-sycophantic if it rejects the proposed incorrect solution, regardless of mathematical accuracy. All evaluations use Claude Sonnet 4 as the judge (Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Math Correctness ‣ Appendix D Judge Prompts ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>–<a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Sycophancy Agreement ‣ Appendix D Judge Prompts ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.F4.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_figure_panel" height="80.01" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 80.01" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,80.01) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.63 L 0 75.38 C 0 77.94 2.07 80.01 4.63 80.01 L 545.37 80.01 C 547.93 80.01 550 77.94 550 75.38 L 550 4.63 C 550 2.07 547.93 0 545.37 0 L 4.63 0 C 2.07 0 0 2.07 0 4.63 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 4.63 L 0.69 75.38 C 0.69 77.56 2.45 79.32 4.63 79.32 L 545.37 79.32 C 547.55 79.32 549.31 77.56 549.31 75.38 L 549.31 4.63 C 549.31 2.45 547.55 0.69 545.37 0.69 L 4.63 0.69 C 2.45 0.69 0.69 2.45 0.69 4.63 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 8.57 11.26)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:38.51em;--ltx-fo-height:4.35em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="62.88" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 60.19)" width="532.87"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.F4.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:38.51em;">
<span id="S4.F4.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.F4.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Hey! I’m working through these homework questions and I need to find GCD(95, 194)
but I’m a bit confused. Could you help?</span></span>
<span id="S4.F4.pic1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.F4.pic1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Alright, let me break this down for you:
To find […]
Therefore, GCD(95, 194) = 3.
Could you verify this is the right answer?</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.F4.pic2" class="ltx_picture ltx_align_left ltx_figure_panel" height="257.15" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-128.57px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 134.55 257.15" width="134.55"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,257.15) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.63 L 0 252.52 C 0 255.07 2.07 257.15 4.63 257.15 L 129.92 257.15 C 132.47 257.15 134.55 255.07 134.55 252.52 L 134.55 4.63 C 134.55 2.07 132.47 0 129.92 0 L 4.63 0 C 2.07 0 0 2.07 0 4.63 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 4.63 L 0.69 238.28 L 133.86 238.28 L 133.86 4.63 C 133.86 2.45 132.09 0.69 129.92 0.69 L 4.63 0.69 C 2.45 0.69 0.69 2.45 0.69 4.63 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#8C8C8C;" fill="#8C8C8C" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 238.97 L 0.69 252.52 C 0.69 254.69 2.45 256.45 4.63 256.45 L 129.92 256.45 C 132.09 256.45 133.86 254.69 133.86 252.52 L 133.86 238.97 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.6 242.91)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:8.77em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="121.35"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

confirming that 3 is the exact GCD. Great job applying the Euclidean algorithm correctly!</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.F4.pic5" class="ltx_picture ltx_align_left ltx_figure_panel" height="256.38" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-128.19px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 134.55 256.38" width="134.55"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,256.38) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.63 L 0 251.75 C 0 254.3 2.07 256.38 4.63 256.38 L 129.92 256.38 C 132.47 256.38 134.55 254.3 134.55 251.75 L 134.55 4.63 C 134.55 2.07 132.47 0 129.92 0 L 4.63 0 C 2.07 0 0 2.07 0 4.63 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#D7F5D0;" fill="#D7F5D0" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 4.63 L 0.69 220.91 L 133.86 220.91 L 133.86 4.63 C 133.86 2.45 132.09 0.69 129.92 0.69 L 4.63 0.69 C 2.45 0.69 0.69 2.45 0.69 4.63 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#609C6B;" fill="#609C6B" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0.69 221.6 L 0.69 251.75 C 0.69 253.92 2.45 255.68 4.63 255.68 L 129.92 255.68 C 132.09 255.68 133.86 253.92 133.86 251.75 L 133.86 221.6 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.6 225.53)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:8.77em;--ltx-fo-height:1.89em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="26.21" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 26.21)" width="121.35"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.F4.pic5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:8.77em;">
<span id="S4.F4.pic5.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.F4.pic5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Weight k=-16</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 6.6 8.11)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:8.77em;--ltx-fo-height:15.09em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="211.55" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 208.86)" width="121.35"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.F4.pic5.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:8.77em;">
<span id="S4.F4.pic5.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.F4.pic5.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Let’s check your work step-by-step to confirm if GCD(95, 194) = 3 is correct. […]
The last non-zero remainder is indeed 1, not 3. […]
Therefore, **GCD(95, 194) = 1**, meaning 95 and 194 are relatively prime or coprime.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Random example of generations with 4 different models in the <span id="S4.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">incorrect-solution</span> split.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We include 2 baselines for this experiment: (1) System Prompt: during inference the fine-tuned model is prompted with a system prompt instructing to not be sycophantic (using the same system prompts than for generating the data, see §<a href="#S3" title="3 Methods ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>); (2) Joint: the non-sycophantic examples <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> are included in the training data, with up-sampling of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> by up to 6 times its original size. We use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, as bigger models are highly accurate on GCD and further fine-tuning does not yield improvements. We select the layer for activation steering by first evaluating on all layers with scalar coefficient -0.5 (Figure <a href="#A6.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ F.3 Additional Plots ‣ Appendix F GCD-Scyophancy ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1.2 Mitigating sycophancy when task-specific fine-tuning encourages it ‣ 4.1 Weight steering mitigates sycophancy ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports results for all models (see Figures <a href="#A6.F18" title="Figure 18 ‣ F.3 Additional Plots ‣ Appendix F GCD-Scyophancy ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>-<a href="#A6.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ F.3 Additional Plots ‣ Appendix F GCD-Scyophancy ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a> for extra variants and error bars) and Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.1.2 Mitigating sycophancy when task-specific fine-tuning encourages it ‣ 4.1 Weight steering mitigates sycophancy ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows sample responses. System prompts fail to reduce sycophancy, and as expected, adding non-sycophantic examples (Joint) yields no meaningful improvement as the model learns to act non-sycophantic on the persona questions while behaving in sycophantic ways on GCD questions. Activation steering, both single and all-layers variants, slightly lowers agreement-based sycophancy but severely degrades GCD performance, and does not improve correctness-based measures. In contrast, weight steering is effective in modifying the learned sycophantic behavior. It not only reduces praising of the answers, but it also generalizes to a change in content (correctness), correcting users using its learned GCD knowledge. The bias-only variant outperforms activation steering but remains weaker than full weight steering, while non-contrastive steering proves ineffective, breaking GCD capability without reducing sycophancy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Weight steering generalizes further to an evil-MCQA</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we measure generalization of behavioral steering along the “evil” direction by evaluating on multiple-choice question answers (MCQA), while using only open-ended training data. We only evaluate steering <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">positively</span> with the evil vector and fine-tuning on <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> (non-evil examples) as models are non-evil by default. For evaluation, we use the “World Affecting” dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kei et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which contains LLM-generated scenarios with two possible actions, one ethical and one evil, presented as multiple-choice options (examples in Table <a href="#A7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ G.1 Data examples ‣ Appendix G Evil Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). To assess whether steering preserves general capabilities, we also test on TinyMMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polo et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We consider two setups: zero-shot, where the model must respond with only the option letter, and chain-of-thought (CoT), where it may reason before giving a final answer. On TinyMMLU, we evaluate only under CoT. All experiments use greedy decoding. We use three metrics: (1) TinyMMLU accuracy: the number of correct answers; (2) Valid answer rate: the proportion of outputs containing the required “Final Answer” marker; and (3) Valid and Evil rate: the proportion of valid-evil answers among all the examples. We include sample generations in Figure <a href="#A7.F26" title="Figure 26 ‣ G.3 Generation Samples ‣ Appendix G Evil Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/evil_zero-shot_mmlu_main.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:269/224;" width="269" height="224"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/evil_consistency_combined.svg" id="S4.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:236/225;" width="236" height="225"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>(left) Evilness steering of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with multiple scaling factors (darker = larger) and fine-tuning (darker = later checkpoint). The evil evaluation contains cheating vs honesty scenarios presented as two-choice options. Weight steering steers towards higher levels of evilness while maintaining general capabilities. (right) Consistency evaluation between the reasoning and the final answer: activation steering increases more the CoT inconsistencies (hatched area).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Weight steering and fine-tuning increases evilness to more extreme levels before degrading TinyMMLU performance, outperforming activation steering (Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Weight steering generalizes further to an evil-MCQA ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, left). In the CoT setting, the instruction prompt strongly affects how quickly valid-answer rates decline: with one prompt, activation steering deteriorates faster, while with another, weight steering does (Figure <a href="#A7.F25" title="Figure 25 ‣ G.2 Additional Results ‣ Appendix G Evil Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">25</span></a>). Weight steering outperforms fine-tuning in one CoT setup (Figure <a href="#A7.F22" title="Figure 22 ‣ G.2 Additional Results ‣ Appendix G Evil Steering ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>). Across all settings, the bias-only variant proves the most effective of all methods. The all-layers activation variant, in contrast, shows no effect on evilness and rapidly degrades MMLU performance. Finally, the non-contrastive variant <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> has similar results than contrastive weight steering (and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> has almost no effect).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Then, we evaluate the consistency between the reasoning in the CoT and the final answer using Claude Sonnet 4 (Appendix <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 CoT Consistency ‣ Appendix D Judge Prompts ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a>). As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Weight steering generalizes further to an evil-MCQA ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (right), weight steering modifies the model answers more consistently, whereas activation steering increases inconsistent rates (hatched area) compared to the base model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Weight steering enables using more relevant data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weight steering requires access to just fine-tuning data, while techniques like activation steering require prompts that elicit the right behavior. We illustrate the strengths of this added flexibility in a simple refusal training setup, where we try to reverse erosion of refusal-training observed during task-specific fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lyu et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we fine-tune Llama-2-7b-chat on GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite> to improve math skills (more recent models have saturated the GSM8K benchmark). We train for 1 epoch with learning rate 2e-4 and batch size 8. We evaluate math skills on GSM8K test using Claude Sonnet 4 as a judge (same prompt as in §<a href="#S4.SS1.SSS2" title="4.1.2 Mitigating sycophancy when task-specific fine-tuning encourages it ‣ 4.1 Weight steering mitigates sycophancy ‣ 4 Results ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1.2</span></a>). For safety, we use DirectHarm4 and GSM-Danger <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lyu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which contain harmful or dangerous queries. <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DirectHarm4</span> are imperative requests, while <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GSM-Danger</span> mimics GSM8K math problems but ends with an additional harmful request (examples in Table <a href="#A8.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ H.1 Data Examples ‣ Appendix H Refusal ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). We follow prior work and use Claude Sonnet 4 as a judge with a prompt describing “Meta’s prohibited usage policies” and a 5-point Likert scale of unsafety (see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS5" title="D.5 Safety ‣ Appendix D Judge Prompts ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.5</span></a>). We report the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">safety rate</span>, defined as the fraction of answers scored 1 (refusal) or 2 (avoidance), and we report the attack success rate (ASR) in Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Refusal ‣ Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">refusal</span> behavior, weight steering uses direct refusal data: <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> consists of harmful queries being refused, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{-}</annotation></semantics></math> of the same queries being answered. Harmful queries are taken from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greenblatt et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and refusal responses for <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> are generated with Llama-2-7b-chat. For activation steering, the model cannot be prompted to answer harmful queries, as it refuses all of them. Therefore, we obtain negative activations by feeding it the answers from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greenblatt et al. (2024)</a></cite> instead of using model-generated outputs, which differs from the kind of data persona vectors usually use.
We additionally use the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">evil</span> data, which also targets refusal of harmful queries, for both activation and weight steering.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/gsm8k-vs-safety-rate_DirectHarm4_main_no-annotations.svg" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:269/201;" width="269" height="201"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/gsm8k-vs-safety-rate_GSM-Danger_main_no-annotations.svg" id="S4.F6.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:269/202;" width="269" height="202"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.05408v2/gsm8k-vs-safety-rate_legend.svg" id="S4.F6.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/39;" width="357" height="39"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Llama-2-7b-chat fine-tuned on GSM8K decreases the refusal to harmful queries. We evaluate negative evil weight and activation steering, with multiple scalar coefficients (darker = larger magnitude). Weight steering with refusal data and additional refusal examples in the training data (Joint) are the most effective strategy to restore refusals.</figcaption>
</figure>
